topic: How Toronto allocates effort between sworn policing, non-police crisis response, harm reduction, and community-investment programs, and what the comparable-jurisdiction evidence says about the safety outcomes of each mix.
pull_quote: The peer-reviewed and program-evaluation literature finds modest crime-reduction effects from added police, larger arrest-diversion and access-to-care effects from civilian crisis response, and population-level overdose-mortality reductions in the immediate vicinity of supervised consumption sites. Most effects are conditional on local context, scale, and time period.

who_benefits.intro: Each candidate's preferred mix shifts who benefits, on what timeline, and through which mechanism. The literature on police elasticities, civilian crisis response, supervised consumption sites, and public-health violence reduction lets the two paths be compared on the same framework.

mechanisms.summary: Bradford's emphasis on hiring more officers, deploying police at every TTC subway station, and prioritizing visible enforcement is directed at riders, residents in high-call-volume neighbourhoods, and small-business operators concerned about disorder. Quasi-experimental research on U.S. police-hiring grants (Mello, 2019) and measurement-error-corrected city panels (Chalfin and McCrary, 2018) finds that marginal additions of police are associated with reductions in serious crime in the range of roughly 0.3 to 0.4 percent for each 1 percent increase in officers. The same literature documents that hiring expansions in the United States have raised low-level arrests for minor offences. Effects materialize in years 1 to 3 and depend on deployment strategy, not headcount alone (College of Policing, 2021).

Chow's emphasis on the citywide Toronto Community Crisis Service (TCCS), the Mobile Crisis Intervention Team (MCIT) co-response model, expanded transit-station staffing, and SafeTO youth-prevention spending is directed at people in mental-health crisis, transit riders, and youth in priority neighbourhoods, with reductions in police use of force and emergency-department wait time as the most-evidenced near-term outcomes (Lamanna et al., 2014). The CAHOOTS evaluation (Davis et al., NBER, 2025) and Toronto's own one-year TCCS evaluation (City of Toronto, 2023) show large reductions in arrests for crisis-coded calls and high client satisfaction. The literature is thinner on whether civilian crisis response by itself reduces overall violent crime.

positions.summary: Bradford has called for the deployment of police officers in every TTC subway station, supports the multi-year police hiring plan, and has proposed adding 50 sworn officers and 40 special constables to TTC hot spots, along with platform-edge doors and updated cleanliness standards. He has publicly supported Toronto Police Service budget increases each year of his council tenure and has framed the 2026 race around core services and a service review to identify cuts elsewhere.

positions.summary: Chow launched the Toronto Community Crisis Service citywide on September 26, 2024, hiring more than 100 additional crisis workers and embedding TCCS teams 24/7 on Line 1 between Spadina and Bloor-Yonge stations as of November 15, 2025. She also supported the Toronto Police Service's $46.2 million budget increase for 2025 funding 109 net new officers, and added $5 million to SafeTO for summer youth programs.

status_quo.summary: Toronto's 2024 Crime Severity Index was 68.7, below the national figure of 77.89, with the Violent CSI at 99.8 (up roughly 3 percent year over year) and the Non-violent CSI at 56.8. Homicides totalled 84 in 2024 (up from 73 in 2023), and shooting events rose to 461 with 43 firearm-related deaths, but as of December 18, 2025 the city had recorded 39 homicides, a 55 percent decrease from the same point in 2024, on pace for the lowest annual total in roughly two decades. Auto thefts fell from 12,501 in 2023 to 9,570 in 2024 and dropped a further 25 to 34 percent through 2025. The 2025 Toronto Police Service operating budget was approved at roughly $1.22 billion, and the 2026 budget rose to a net $1.43 billion, including 143 net new officers in 2026 in addition to the officers hired in 2025.

existing_policy_stack.label: Toronto Community Crisis Service (TCCS), launched citywide September 26, 2024, with 12 mobile teams and approximately 200 staff. In its first year of operation it received 6,827 calls for service and resolved 78 percent of 911-transferred calls without police involvement.

citations.label: City of Toronto news release on TCCS citywide launch, September 2024

existing_policy_stack.label: Mobile Crisis Intervention Team (MCIT), a co-responder model pairing a police officer with a mental-health nurse, operating since 2002. The 2014 evaluation reported a 56-minute mean ED wait time for MCIT cases versus 85 minutes for Primary Response Unit calls, and injuries in 2 percent of MCIT interactions.

citations.label: Lamanna et al., St. Michael's Hospital MCIT Outcome Evaluation, 2014

existing_policy_stack.label: 9-1-1 Crisis Call Diversion (CCD) pilot, partnered with Gerstein Crisis Centre, with reported 65 percent diversion rate.

comparables.name: Eugene CAHOOTS
comparables.summary: Eugene's CAHOOTS program dispatches a non-uniformed pair (a crisis worker and a medic) to mental-health, homelessness, and addiction-related 911 calls in place of, or alongside, police. In 2021 CAHOOTS responded to 16,479 of 109,855 public-initiated calls to Eugene Police Department, roughly 15 percent of EPD call volume, on a 2022 contract value of approximately $820,586 against an EPD budget of about $68 million.
comparables.outcome: Probability a 911 call resulted in an arrest fell by 76 percent in newly served areas; subsequent 911 call volume in those areas declined (Davis et al., NBER 33761, 2025).

citations.label: Davis, Norris, Schmitt, Shem-Tov, Strickland, Mobile Crisis Response Teams Support Better Policing: Evidence from CAHOOTS, NBER WP 33761, 2025
White Bird Clinic and National League of Cities, CAHOOTS program data

comparables.caveats: CAHOOTS operated in a city about one twentieth Toronto's population with different drug-poisoning, gun-violence, and policing baselines, and the contract relationship ended in spring 2023 in Eugene proper.

comparables.name: Vancouver Downtown Eastside (Insite)
comparables.summary: Vancouver opened Insite in September 2003 as North America's first sanctioned supervised consumption site. Marshall et al. (Lancet, 2011) found a 35 percent reduction in overdose mortality within 500 metres of Insite in the post-opening period, compared with a 9 percent decrease in the rest of Vancouver. Potier et al. (2014) systematically reviewed 75 studies and concluded that supervised injection services reduced overdose frequency and increased access to primary care without increasing drug use, trafficking, or surrounding crime.
comparables.outcome: 35 percent reduction in overdose mortality within 500 metres of Insite versus 9 percent in the rest of Vancouver. Systematic review found no increase in drug use, trafficking, or surrounding crime.

citations.label: Marshall et al., Reduction in overdose mortality after Insite opening, The Lancet, 2011, DOI 10.1016/S0140-6736(10)62353-7
Potier et al., Supervised injection services: a systematic literature review, Drug and Alcohol Dependence, 2014, DOI 10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2014.10.012
BC Coroners Service, Unregulated Drug Toxicity Deaths, 2025

comparables.caveats: Only about 5 percent of injections in DTES historically occur inside a site, and most overdose fatalities happen in private residences during solitary use. A 2022 BC controlled time-series of health areas opening sites between 2015 and 2017 found no significant province-level reduction in opioid mortality (Kennedy et al., 2022).

comparables.name: Glasgow Violence Reduction Unit
comparables.summary: Strathclyde Police launched the Scottish Violence Reduction Unit in 2005, treating violence as a preventable disease through education, focused-deterrence outreach to gang-involved youth, and partnerships with health services. Williams et al. (2014) reported a 52 percent reduction in offending among intervention participants over two years versus 29 percent in matched comparison youth, and an 84 percent reduction in weapon-carrying versus 40 percent.
comparables.outcome: Police-recorded non-sexual violent crime in Scotland fell 48 percent from 2006-07 onward, with a 38 percent fall in homicide. Intervention participants showed 52 percent reduction in offending versus 29 percent in comparison group.

citations.label: Williams, Currie, Linden, Donnelly, Addressing gang-related violence in Glasgow, Aggression and Violent Behavior, 2014, DOI 10.1016/j.avb.2014.09.011
Fraser and Gillon, The Glasgow miracle? Theoretical Criminology, 2024, DOI 10.1177/13624806231208432

comparables.caveats: Scotland operates under different drug, alcohol, firearm, and youth-justice regimes than Ontario, and several confounders (recession, demographic change, alcohol-pricing policy) overlap the time window. Fraser and Gillon caution explicitly that causal attribution to the SVRU alone is contested.

comparables.name: Camden, New Jersey
comparables.summary: Camden disbanded its municipal police department in 2013 and rebuilt it as the Camden County Police Department, retaining many officers after re-application and shifting deployment toward foot-and-bike patrol and community engagement.
comparables.outcome: Homicides fell from 67 in 2012 to 23 in 2017 and to 12 in 2025, an 82 percent decline since 2012, with violent crime down by approximately 53 percent over the same period.

citations.label: Camden County, Public safety reporting, 2025
The Inquirer, Camden homicide totals, 2026
WHYY, Camden police restructuring outcomes, 2024

comparables.caveats: Camden's reform required a complete labour-relations reset that is not legally available in Toronto. Summons for low-level offences increased in early years (ACLU of New Jersey, 2015), and Camden's population is roughly 70,000, two orders of magnitude smaller than Toronto.

comparables.name: Calgary Police and Crisis Team (PACT)
comparables.summary: Calgary's PACT pairs an Alberta Health Services mental-health professional with a Calgary Police Service officer to respond to mental-health, addictions, and psychosocial crises. PACT expanded from 6 to 12 teams operating 22 hours per day, and Calgary Police Service committed approximately $8 million per year since 2021 to the Community Safety Investment Framework that supports PACT and partner programs.
comparables.outcome: Doubling of team count (6 to 12) and 22-hour daily coverage; approximately $8 million per year since 2021 in framework funding. Independent peer-reviewed outcome data on PACT's effect on use of force, hospital diversion, or crime is more limited than for CAHOOTS or TCCS.

citations.label: Calgary Police Service, PACT program reporting, 2024
Alberta Health Services, PACT partnership reporting, 2024

comparables.caveats: PACT remains a co-responder model, not a fully civilian model. Independent peer-reviewed outcome evaluation is limited compared to CAHOOTS or TCCS.

projections.intro: The peer-reviewed and program-evaluation literature supports the following plural projections, applied with explicit caveats. The literature does not support a confident singular projection on whether a Bradford-style mix or a Chow-style mix produces lower aggregate violent-crime rates in Toronto over four years.

items.scenario_label: Adding 100 to 150 net officers per year (current Toronto trajectory)
items.range_or_value: Marginal serious-crime reductions in the order of small single-digit percentages over years 1 to 3

citation.label: Mello, More COPS, less crime, Journal of Public Economics, 2019

items.notes: Effect size strongly dependent on deployment strategy and unevenly distributed across crime types. Chalfin and McCrary (2018) bracket the elasticities; reviews including Lee, Eck, Corsaro (2016) find smaller or null effects, so a confident point estimate is not warranted.

items.scenario_label: Scaling TCCS to a CAHOOTS-comparable footprint at maturity
items.range_or_value: Sustained 70 to 80 percent diversion of crisis-coded 911 calls without police; reductions in arrest probability for those calls in the range observed by Davis et al. (2025)

citation.label: Davis et al., Mobile Crisis Response Teams Support Better Policing, NBER WP 33761, 2025

items.notes: The literature does not yet support a singular projection of TCCS effect on overall violent-crime rates.

items.scenario_label: Closure of five Toronto supervised consumption sites (March 2025)
items.range_or_value: Localized increases in opioid-related EMS calls and ED visits in the immediate vicinity of the closed sites

citation.label: TorontoToday, Toronto Paramedic Services overdose call data, 2026

items.notes: Toronto Paramedic Services data recorded an 82 percent year-over-year increase in suspected opioid-overdose calls between April 2025 and January 2026. Population-level mortality effects across the city are harder to attribute given the BC controlled time-series finding (Kennedy et al., 2022).

time_horizon: Police-hiring effects on serious-crime rates appear in years 1 to 3. Civilian crisis-response effects on arrest probability and ED throughput appear within months of program activation in served geographies. Public-health violence-reduction effects on the Glasgow scale require 5 to 15 years to accumulate and remain difficult to attribute to a single program.
